Psychotherapy Research11(3), 239-257, 2001

Therapy Amount and Outcome of Inpatient Psychodynamic Treatment of Eating Disorders in Germany: Data from a Multicenter Study

Horst Käuchele, Hans Kordy and Matthias Richard

The present study investigates (a) factors that determine length of treatment and (b) the effect of treatment duration and other factors on outcome for patients with eating disorders. In this observational study, the symptomatic status of 1,171 patients was observed for 2.5 years after admission to 1 of 43 participating hospitals. Treatment and outcome were modelled using hierarchical linear models and logistic regression. To control for possible confounding factors, propensity score adjustment was used. Treatment modalities, especially length and intensity, varied considerably between and within hospitals and were related to patient characteristics to a very small degree. At 2.5 year follow-up, 33% of anorexia patients and 25% of bulimia patients were symptom free. Length of treatment showed a weak effect on outcome and only in interaction with other patient characteristics of relevance, whereas treatment intensity was not related to outcome. Implications for treatment planning are discussed.



Psychotherapy Research11(3), 295-309, 2001

Sounds of Silence in Psychotherapy: The Categorization of Clients' Pauses

Heidi M. Levitt

Empirical studies examined silences in psychotherapy by measuring the duration of pauses and studying this variable as a homogeneous factor. This approach produced a body of inconclusive findings dealing with the relation between silences and therapeutic outcome or alliance. In the present study, interpersonal process recall interviews of 7 clients' self-reported experiences of in-session pauses were analysed. A qualitative analysis, based on grounded theory methodology, was used. In this inductive process, researches are guided by the analysis of data to develop an understanding of phenomena grounded in empirical observation. A pausing inventory of 7 categories was generated, reflecting an understanding of silences as heterogeneous phenomena, and included disengaged pauses, emotional pauses, interactional pauses, reflexive pauses, expressive pauses, associational pauses, and mnemonic pauses. This categorization of pauses can facilitate attunement to client pausing experiences both in future research and in the performance of psychotherapy.

[[RunningHead]]

Editorial

Jean Arundale

Jean Arundale

[BJP@jarundale.demon.co.uk]

Jean Arundale  

IN THIS ISSUE …

Winnicott placed a high value on the life-affirming and expressive qualities of the human imagination. Richard Frankel writes of how Winnicott viewed the relationship between fantasy, reality and the transitional shared third space, illustrated by his case study, The Piggle.

When does a pathological culture give rise to new forms of madness? The manic lifestyles of youth and their influence on the unconscious psychic life of the individual are the subject of Giovanni Starace's article.

Research into how psychotherapy works and whether it is effective is demanded by today's culture, but can it be undertaken in a clinical setting without interfering with and upsetting the therapeutic relationship? A group at the TMSI, Christopher Clulow, Avi Shmueli, Christopher Vincent and Christopher Evans, introduced a research protocol into the procedures of couple therapy that became acceptable to clinicians, yielding better understanding of links between attachment patterns of couples and their conflict management tactics.

Engaging people from ethnic minorities in psychotherapy currently preoccupies many service providers and brings up questions of cultural matching. Jaya Gowrisunkur, Erica Burman and Kanta Walker report on a brief dynamic therapy with a Pakistani Muslim man conducted by a non-Muslim Asian woman, working in the patient's native language.

Men who have been sexually abused in childhood can be significantly helped by psychodynamic group therapy as reported by Audrey Morrison and Linda Treliving. The men, all with severe symptoms and personality problems, improved in terms of emotional distress, interpersonal sensitivity, depression and psychoticism as measured by the SCL 90.

Mothers and babies have been treated together in both group and individual therapy with good results. Two contributions in this issue feature mother and baby therapy: Jessica James writes of a group which evolved into a safe, reliable ‘group-mother’ through cycles of collapse and recovery. Then our Special Clinical Commentary organized by Sue Robinson and Janine Sternberg features clinical material from mother-baby sessions, commented upon by therapists from The Anna Freud Centre, The Tavistock Clinic and The Tavistock Infant/Child Therapy Team and child therapists Miranda Davies and Luis Rodríguez de la Sierra.

Connection and Catastrophe, Hope and Despair in our Borderline World

Penelope Campling

Penelope Campling

Francis Dixon Lodge, Gipsy Lane, Leicester LE5 0TD. [email: Penelope.Campling@leicspart.nhs.uk]

Penelope Campling  

Despair is the absence of connections or the severance of connections and the consequent sense of emptiness and impotence. Hope is about connecting, relating, being part of a healthy matrix and the consequent sense of agency that can come from this.

This talk explores the particular quality of disconnectedness in our more disturbed patients where hope and despair move in cycles without any sense of a functioning centre that can keep hold of the pieces and understand how they fit together. Parallels are drawn between our patients' internal worlds and the external world in which we are located and work.

Developing a sense of personal agency within a meaningful social matrix in a therapeutic community is contrasted to the state where the organization is always on the edge of unpredictable catastrophe and patients remain in a condition of despairing helplessness.

Clinical Commentary XXX on Parent-Child Work

Sue Robinson and Janine Sternberg

Janine Sternberg

Janine Sternberg  

In this special clinical commentary on parent-child work, I would like firstly to thank Louise Emanuel (Head of Under Five's Service at the Tavistock Clinic) for her efforts to make the whole piece possible. Secondly, my co-editor, Janine Sternberg, for her efforts in producing the clinical contribution and commentators and Alicia Etchegoyen for suggesting the whole idea. I hoped that this edition might be a step towards an approach which illustrates how a variety of contributors, some even from the same theoretical schools, exemplify different understanding of clinical material.

Sue Robinson

I too would like to express gratitude to Louise Emanuel for helping to make the piece happen. The contributors are all leading clinicians in this special field of parent-child work and many of them take the opportunity frequently to discuss case material ‘across the theoretical boundaries’. We chose to have more contributors than the usual three, to show the complexity of this apparently simple work.

Janine Sternberg

Clinical Material

The family consisted of Ms S, Owen, aged 3 years, and Susan, aged 8 weeks. Father, an alcoholic, had left the family when Owen was 1 year old - the couple had had a violent relationship. Mother's new partner had been in prison for eight months. She had a poor relationship with her own family. Owen was referred by a health visitor to the Under Fives Counselling Service because of his disruptive, violent behaviour, particularly towards his mother and his baby sister. During the first of five sessions Susan slept throughout, while Owen hit and kicked at mother or me when we tried to set firm boundaries. Ms S is an attractive but careworn woman and Owen is a burly, rather thick-set child.

Second of Five Sessions

They were a little late and Ms S came in apologizing, saying that the baby had had her injection. Owen came in, keen to see his drawings again and showed me quickly that he had hurt his lip. Mum explained that Owen had ‘gotten into a state’ and had bitten her, and then had fallen and hurt his lip.

The Spirit of Sanity by Neville Symington. Published by Karnac, London, 2001; 204 pages; £19.95 paperback.

Janet Sayers

Janet Sayers

Janet Sayers  

Psychoanalysis and religion can be inspiring. They can also be deadly. Perhaps this is why psychoanalysis has eschewed religion. Born of the triumph of nineteenth-century material and scientific progress, psychoanalysis seems the very antithesis of religion. Nevertheless in his book, Emotion and Spirit, Neville Symington began to bring them together.

Maybe his success in doing so contributed to his being invited to run a weekend conference on the subject at the Tavistock Clinic in September 1999. Its proceedings constitute the material of The Spirit of Sanity. In it Symington emphasizes the shared concern of psychoanalysis and religion with the life of the psyche or spirit. But what brings the spirit to life? Hegel described it - consciousness at least - as brought into being through its recognition by the consciousness of another. Winnicott described it as brought alive through ‘primary maternal preoccupation’, through the mother lovingly identifying with, and thereby discovering and nourishing, her baby's spirited imagination - or illusion - of what is already there. Bion described the mother transforming and animating the baby's inanimate sense data - ‘beta elements’ - by dreaming them into ‘alpha elements’ to furnish his conscious and unconscious mental life. Symington likens this process to mysticism. Through her ‘loving act’ of ‘related-to-the-object’ contemplation of the ‘actual contours’ of her baby, he says, she finds and brings alive the spirit that is both infinite and unique to him (pp. 65, 73).

But what happens when this loving act is absent? The vacuum may then be filled, says Symington, by making a god of oneself or others. Freud called this figure the superego. Either way, through being consciously or unconsciously projected or repressed as a reified or deified person or thing, the spirit becomes senseless. It loses meaning and life. Reviving it is painful. For it means shouldering freedom - the counterpart of the determinism and necessity of material reality. It means shouldering the responsibility of choosing and deciding. The burden, Symington claims, is conveyed in Piero della Francesca's painting of Christ with downcast eyes on being anointed by John the Baptist.

Feeling the Ground

John Ryder

John Ryder

Thurmaston Lane, Leicester LE5 0TA. [email: johnryder@doctors.net.uk]

John Ryder  

The nature of everything is open, empty and naked like the sky.

Luminous emptiness, without centre or circumference: the pure naked Rigpa dawns.

(The Tibetan Book of the Dead, Fremantle 1975)

The occasion was the first session of a ‘median group experience’ with the purpose to focus on itself, open to practitioners working in the NHS, private and voluntary sectors. Various members of the group already knew some of the others to a greater or lesser degree but, as a new venture, the element of the unknown was heightened and, as the door closed, silence loomed loud.

I became conscious of a kind of global anxiety, with roused senses and deep uncertainty. How to think, or not think? To speak, or not to speak? If to speak, then what to say? Personal revelation? Comment on the group? Or wait and see. The longer it went on, the more grew the sense that in saying nothing when something could be said was to withhold a contribution to ease group tension. Alternatively, the sooner something was said, the sooner this pregnant emptiness would be delivered from itself.

Beginnings are unique. Anything is possible. It is like being at the summit when any descent can be used. As the steps go down, the route becomes increasingly formed and limited. It could have been that valley, but we have chosen this one. I wanted to linger on the giddy heights, to see in all directions, but to do so would be to refuse to engage in the collective process in time, and a direction must be chosen. James Taylor

James Taylor

Leeds

James Taylor  

Occasionally, in my clinical work, clients have recounted blind dates following adverts placed and searches made through contact magazines. Invariably a certain something had sufficiently drawn their attention and provoked their expectations, demanding imagination be met by experience. I was attracted to this collection in much the same way and so, perhaps unsurprisingly, the map only partially represented the territory. Putatively, Sexuality: Psychoanalytic Perspectives is a book in which the subject of sexuality is comprehensively introduced, developed and ‘brought up to date for the twenty-first century’. To this end, according to the promotional material, ‘a range of distinguished contributors challenge the view that sexuality is nothing other than historically and culturally determined’.

I was intrigued by such an advertisement, particularly as it excluded the legend ‘GSOH’. How, I wondered, could sexuality be brought up to date? But perhaps this wasn't to be the project and instead understandings of sexuality would be updated. Yet, if this was to be, how could it be achieved through the lens of psychoanalysis without significant reference to historical and cultural perspectives? After all, psychoanalysis, like so many new flames, moves on.

Positive or Negative History of Childhood Sexual Abuse among Problem Drinkers: Relationship to Substance use Disorders and Psychiatric Comorbidity

José Martínez-Raga, Francis Keaney, E. Jane Marshall, David Ball, David Best and John Strang

Background Victims of childhood sexual abuse (CSA) show higher rates of several psychiatric and substance abuse disorders in adulthood. High rates of CSA have been reported in alcohol- or drug-dependent patients presenting to treatment. However, there is a paucity of European research with regard to inpatient alcohol-dependent populations.

Aims The aim was to describe the prevalence of CSA in a UK sample of alcohol-dependent inpatients admitted over a 3-year period to a specialist alcohol unit; also to identify socio-demographic, alcohol and other substance use-related variables, and co-morbid psychiatric disorders associated with CSA.

Method Clinical and socio-demographic data and information on childhood sexual abuse (CSA) were collected from 414 admissions, between September 1995 and September 1998, to the Specialist Alcohol Inpatient Unit.

Results In the total sample of 414 subjects, 52 had experienced CSA. Of the 311 male subjects included in the study, 20 (6.4%) had experienced CSA. Of the 103 female subjects in the study sample, 32 (31.1%) disclosed having a history of CSA (CSA-females). Women victims of CSA were more likely to be non-white, to have a positive family history of alcoholism and to have fewer years of excessive drinking prior to admission. They were also significantly more likely to have a lifetime diagnosis of depressive anxiety and eating disorders, as well as being more likely to have a co-morbid post-traumatic stress disorder and a borderline personality disorder. Male victims had significantly higher Alcohol Problems Questionnaire (APQ) scores, were more likely to live alone, to be single, separated, divorced or widowed and to have a post-traumatic stress disorder and a borderline personality disorder.

Editorial

Jean Arundale

Jean Arundale

[BJP@jarundale.demon.co.uk]

Jean Arundale  

In This Issue …

Papers from a conference entitled God and the Unconscious: A Contribution to the New Dialogue between Psychotherapy and Religion are presented herein. David Black introduces and contextualizes the themes, signalling the potential for religions to unify and to encompass opposites. Christopher MacKenna speaks of enduring religious symbols embedded in the unconscious. He examines the process of psychological-cum-spiritual development found in the Bible as a central dynamic underlying the text, and presents case material relating to a patient's faith. Rodney Bomford argues that levels of discourse in Christian faith form the logic of the unconscious, relating to the theories of Matte Blanco. He notes that the powerful mystical experiences of God are found in the deepest unconscious layers and are shared by many faiths.

We include further contributions on the topic.

In the Jewish faith the rabbi is a teacher of religious wisdom, a storyteller and a healer. Howard Cooper draws comparisons between the rabbi and the psychotherapist, featuring bodily experience and the countertransference. As a Muslim and a psychoanalyst, Fakhry Davids writes of religious and racial stereotyping that produced polarized responses to the world crisis following September 11th.

In Irish mythology there are ancient tales of madness that describe the psychotic state in terms parallel with those of Freud and Klein. However, these narratives of the ‘wild man’ outside society, tales of the battlefield, passion, poetics, melancholia, and object loss, writes Brendan McMahon, are less concerned with inner causes, but more with the social context, the rejection of the human by the subject, and his therapeutic return to the social world.

Paul Schimmel explores the way in which T.S. Eliot's passions and suffering were linked with his creative expressions and constituted the raw materials for his art. Eliot's own personal Waste Land, the period between his first marriage and his breakdown, which, coinciding with the completion of the poem, suggests that his poetry was vital to the transmuting analytic work that led toward the slow integration of his self over the last 30 years of his life.

New ‘Normalities’, New ‘Madnesses’

Giovanni Starace

Giovanni Starace

Corso Vittorio Emanuele 167/4, 80121 Napoli, Italy. [email: gio.starace@libero.it]

Giovanni Starace  

A few decades ago a great deal of attention was given to the narcissistic syndromes, as well as to the culture of narcissism. Basic difficulties and deficits in the subjects were emphasized, more so than the drive to self-sufficiency. These pathological manifestations are certainly still alive today, but other manifestations tend to characterize this ‘culture of narcissism’ even more. The drive to consumerism, the fast use and obsolescence of things, difficulties of expectation, the over-estimation of material goods in definition of the self, an inclination to risk-taking, and a compulsiveness of action are examples of them. Such manifestations find expression in drug addiction, the ‘consumption’ of sex, gambling, compulsive shopping, abuse of alcohol, and pathological behaviour toward food. These expressions of discomfort are apparently distinct, but they are also very ‘close to the culture’ and they express the environment from which they emerge. The article includes clinical material from private praxis, and institutional work with drug addicts.

Marilyn Mathew

London

Marilyn Mathew  

In their new book, Jung and Film, Christopher Hauke and Ian Alister have brought together a collection of analysts, therapists and academics from the

120

world of film and media to comment on the moving image from a Jungian perspective. The result is a stimulating, thought-provoking and varied book that invites one to take both a broader look at the cultural commentary of contemporary film and look closer at the detail and themes running through particular movies. The book pays close attention to symbols and symbolic attitudes and, for a medium where art might be sacrificed to commercial interests, maintains typical Jungian links with depth, myth and teleological meaning.

Three sections follow the introduction. Part I, entitled ‘A Jungian Perspective’, includes chapters by Don Fredericksen on ‘Jung/sign/symbol/film’, Lydia Lennihan on ‘The alchemy of Pulp Fiction’ and Pat Berry on ‘Image in motion’. These three opening chapters set the scene for the book, introducing the Jungian and post-Jungian views that encourage a deeper analysis of popular culture and complex thought, and are primarily aimed at those who are not totally familiar with a Jungian point of view. The concise glossary at the end of the book will also be helpful if some of the terminology used is unfamiliar. I particularly enjoyed Pat Berry's chapter. She makes the point that film began at the same time as depth psychology, and goes on to state that art requires and responds to pathology within the context of our modern world, film being one way in which we become more aware, collectively, of the objective psyche at work.

Part II, entitled ‘Four Films and a Director’, includes chapters by John Hollwitz on ‘The Grail quest and Field of Dreams’, Jane Ryan on ‘Dark City’, Don Williams on ‘“If you could have seen what I've seen with your eyes …”: post-human psychology and Blade Runner’, ‘2001: A Space Odyssey: a classical reading’ and Christopher Hauke on ‘“Let's go back to finding out who we are”: men, Unheimlich and returning home in the films of Steven Spielberg’. These chapters are terrific. They explore each film in depth, in relation to Jungian concepts. John Hollwitz picks up on the way an ordinary field in the middle of nowhere in the Midwest, where Field of Dreams had been set, spontaneously acquired numinous symbolic meaning and attracts hundreds of visitors. Jane Ryan views Dark City as a description of individuation and the hero's necessary path through the darkness and misery of nigredo. Don Williams considers a similar quest depicted in Blade Runner, which focuses on what it means to be human by exploring the idea of the heirosgamos or sacred marriage. Finally, in this section, Christopher Hauke takes a look at six of Steven Spielberg's films and includes quotes from televised interviews to think about how one director's struggle to deal with his own psychological issues can mirror shifts in the broader culture. He makes an important plea - that ‘popular’, ‘escapist’ or ‘commercial’ films should be taken seriously as presenting the unconscious needs of the objective psyche.

Roger Kennedy  

I can highly recommend this book which covers a very complex and difficult field of confidentiality in mental health. The book explores the theoretical and practical implications of confidentiality and disclosure of professionals working with those suffering from mental health problems. This complex field is covered by 13 different presentations by various professionals from different perspectives including child and adult psychiatry, forensic psychiatry, criminal law, community psychiatry, psychoanalysis, psychotherapy, social work, nursing and philosophy. While the problem with collections of papers is often a lack of coherence and focus, the advantage in this case is that the many problems of confidentiality in mental health can be explored from a variety of different angles, opening up many questions for which there are often no clear answers.

There is clearly more and more emphasis these days on professionals having to be open about what they do. In the past there has been too much secrecy and too much use of professional jargon and mystique in order to maintain professional power. This has resulted in a number of scandals which have mainly come to light in the field of medical and surgical practice. However, the issues involved are also very relevant to those dealing with mental health in adults, adolescents and children. One could say that the secrecy was a side effect of the need for confidentiality. Along with the need now for professionals to be more open there has been the danger of the erosion of confidentiality. This is particularly now a problem due to the fact that most professionals work in multi-disciplinary teams. The advantage of this is the ability to share ideas and to share stresses and strains but the danger of losing confidentiality is that much greater. The professional is often then caught in a difficult situation between, on the one hand, trying to maintain confidentiality and, on the other hand, having to share information. At the same time there is the constant push towards more and more disclosure and openness as a result of the public's concern about all kinds of medical scandals.

Response to Public Attack on Freud and his Daughter Anna

Isobel Hunter-Brown

Isobel Hunter-Brown

Leicester

Isobel Hunter-Brown  

Dear Editor

The Sunday evening TV series on The Self in the Twentieth Century which ended on 7 April 2002 brought us salutory enlightenment as to how big business and, latterly, politicians have exploited for their own ends the often alien and unwelcome theories of Freud about how human psychology is rooted in our physical constitution. Their success in so doing suggests that Freud was right.

However, to blame him for the way his views have been used is surely a case of ‘shooting the messenger’. These matters were in the public domain around two decades before Bernais explained them to those interested in advertising. How Freud himself used them was to promote greater self-awareness in his patients so that they would no longer be blindly driven by desires but be able to lead more integrated lives with free use of reason. In the series, whatever possible in the way of accusation was raked up without full consideration of the facts, in order to discredit Freud and his followers.

His daughter, Anna, was particularly horrendously and misleadingly portrayed. It is suggested that her treatment of maladjusted children was aimed at imposing conformity on society. In fact, it released her small patients from unbearable conflicts which had prevented them from pleasurably participating in ordinary childhood activities and learning. They may also have been preventing others from doing so.

Had Anna Freud been more regardful of her reputation and less concerned to try to help her friend's suicidal daughter, she would not have taken the distraught young woman into her home. Earlier, the girl's childhood must, I think, have been terrorized by Hitler's persecution, or traumatized by it through attempts to shield her from it, perhaps by separation from her family. There are people whose psychological state is analogous to that of someone with terminal cancer, whose doctors are not blamed for their death.

This country owes Anna Freud a debt of gratitude for the wartime nursery she ran in London for about 100 babies or children separated from their parents in the Blitz. A wise toleration and understanding of emotions and motivations characterized the nursery. The exchanges between ‘housemothers’ and children are preserved in its archives. One of these ‘mothers’, Ilse Hellman, a psychoanalyst, wrote a delightful book about ‘her’ children entitled From War Babies to Grandmothers - a span indicating life-long affection.

Kate White

Kate White

London

Kate White  

Christopher Clulow has set out to bring together 17 contributors to write about psychotherapy with couples from an attachment perspective. The book aims to provide a framework for assessing and working with people in both secure and insecure partnerships. It includes the viewpoints of both contemporary clinical practice and research.

When I was asked to do this review my first thought was, like many individual psychotherapists, what do I know about couples' psychotherapy? On reflection I realized that I do work with many individuals for whom the issues around their couple relationship can be the focus of their therapy. Exploration of the joys but, sadly, more often the disappointments, preoccupations of hopelessness, the painful dilemmas and longings for intimacy within a relationship can be central concerns. Often these experiences are re-enacted within the therapeutic relationship giving an opportunity to explore their complex unconscious origins. As a psychotherapist whose work is informed by attachment theory, and with a spirit of enquiry and some trepidation I embarked on reading and reviewing this book.

Clulow identifies the aims of this book as twofold. The first is to develop further dialogue between clinical practice and research. He sees participation in research as having the potential for therapeutic effects. He identifies his stance as a couple therapist as one of a collaborator in a research endeavour, the focus of which is the the participants' exploration of their different experiences and subjectivities in the therapeutic relationship. This is a very timely contribution to the discussion.

The book illustrates well the ways in which attachment research can inform practice. For example, Clulow suggests that the Adult Attachment Interview categories of states of mind which are ‘unresolved’ or ‘unclassifiable’ in relation to trauma or loss are a way of identifying the vulnerabilities of couples whose strategies for managing anxiety have broken down. ‘This research provides us as clinicians with useful tools in enlarging the area of clinical insight as well as indicating research possibilities for broadening the empirical basis of our knowledge about couple relationships.’ Whilst I would endorse the former, I do think that the latter comment reveals a lack of confidence in the validity of our own very particular and unique forms of clinical knowing. It points to a need for dialogue amongst equals, and not a search for what may be felt to be the assumed superiority of what are called empirically tested truths.

Crooked Angels by Carol Lee. Published by Century, London, 2001; 275 pages; £9.99.

Jan Woolf

Jan Woolf

London

Jan Woolf  

Carol Lee wakes one morning to find her body null and void. Her head is as ‘heavy as a waterlogged football’ atop a body of separate pieces that her useless spine cannot coordinate. Trapped in a ‘cage of pain’, a few hours later she is attacked by ‘electric shocks’ shooting through her arms - the ‘big guns’. So she describes the literally shocking beginning to her illness. She has to give up work and become a tenant in her own house - an uneasy parallel to the tenancy her mind now has in her body. After some aborted treatments and learning to sit so perfectly still that she can't feel the pain, she writes;

Now, the outside of me, where my skin meets the world, is as far away as the top of a wave is to the seabed. I've gone and arrived at the same time. I'm relieved, first of all, to be rid of the pain, and also afraid. If this is madness will I find my way back? But it can't be. Madness is bedlam, chaos betrayal and this isn't. I have arrived, at last, at the bottom of myself, a place so vast you would never want to be on top again. It's limitless and here, on the ocean floor, sorrow and grief have no place. Nor the woman who typed a thousand words before breakfast. (p. 28)

This is fine writing. I'm not making a gratuitous point, for her book is as much about her formation as a writer as it is the journey of discovery to the source of her illness. Friends introduce her to the osteopath Renzo Molinari who sets her on the path of psychic enquiry through reliving her childhood. Interspliced with her autobiography is a superb account of how writing helped her survive a childhood lived through the emotional fallout of a World War Two fighter pilot father, a passive, unprotecting mother and a damaged grandmother. Her head ‘a den of secret resistance’, she used and developed language to control her world and protect her from her father and his evocation of a controlling, punishing God (for whom she wanted to be a good girl). So the buckling of a little girl's spirit and the process of storing painful memories in her body are integral to the formation of Carol Lee as a writer. Writing warded off mental breakdown as a child, but physical breakdown was latent.

Clinical Studies in Neuro-Psychoanalysis: Introduction to A Depth Neuropsychology by Karen Kaplan-Solms and Mark Solms, with A Foreword by Arnold Z. Pfeffer. Published by Karnac Books, London, 2000; 308 Pages; £19.95 Paperback.

Joseph Schwartz

Joseph Schwartz

London

Joseph Schwartz  

To an extent the authors of this important book have done their project a disservice with their subtitle Introduction to a Depth Neuropsychology. Psychoanalytic clinicians who are not familiar with the results and terminology of neuropsychology will, I fear, be overwhelmed by the technical detail and the state of the art argument that is on offer. The book is not an introduction. What it is is a report of work in progress. I propose to review it as such taking seriously the authors' plea:

From the outset we had a lot to learn about both of the fields we wanted to combine in this research. We trust readers will not judge these early steps too harshly, especially with respect to our handling of psychoanalytic technique. (p. ix)

Based on lectures and previously published material going back to 1993, the book does not have the excitement of current developments in neuro-psychoanalysis so well communicated by Mark Solms in his recent lectures at the Anna Freud Centre. But it does have important clinical work by Karen Kaplan-Solms describing the psychoanalytic treatment of patients with specific brain injuries. This work is of general psychoanalytic interest because it sheds light on the neurological correlations of subjective experience. We see that damage to the left frontal and anterior temporal lobes does not impair normal mourning of the loss of function while damage to the right side of the brain in the parietal-occipital lobes does. The description of the treatment of 12 patients will also be of interest to clinicians who work with disability although, of course, there will be inevitable disagreements over technique and approach associated with different orientations.

As a work in progress, what can the general clinical reader come away with? What seems firm is the importance of A.R. Luria's theoretical framework of dynamic localization. The philosopher Jerry Fodor has likened traditional narrow localization studies as being similar to specifying the location of the carburettor in a car. Who cares really whether it is on the left or right side of the car as long as we know that it mixes air and petrol into a combustible mixture prior to entering the cylinder? What dynamic localization makes clear is that the various brain regions participate dynamically in the process of interest rather than being the static location of mourning and loss. Secondly, it seems clear that the timeless illogicality of dream juxtapositions can be attributed to the fact that, as revealed in MRI studies, the prefrontal lobes of the brain do not contribute in the dreaming state.

Marietta Marcus

Marietta Marcus

Marietta Marcus  

On hearing, seeing or reading current events one is bombarded with news that would need one's compassion. Time for reflection is needed, but the next news item and then the next practical task await attention. The horrendous impact has to wait until later. Ovid's myths have forced me to take time and look at some of them. I believe the analytically trained mind can help. The theatre too has power to influence. Given power, artist and writers may act in politics and over time achieve choice, compromise or resolution of conflict.

The London performance of ten Tales from Ovid at the Young Vic drew me to Waterloo on a hot summer afternoon in 2000. The theatre in the round was mostly black and dark. The stage was covered in white sand, a piece of shiny plastic in the middle and a well to one side. Smoke was coming from behind broken walls. Put a rope down on the plastic and you have the pool of Narcissus, when required. Five myths on either side of the interval smoothly followed each other with transformations of the stage in front of our eyes. One's imagination was assisted by joyful music, speech, deafening thunder and dramatic silences.

To start with, the mood was playful.

The Psychoanalyst's Values and Countertransference

Romano Biancoli

On the subject of countertransference we attempt to establish a line of continuity between Freud's own expression ‘blind spot’ and Fromm's idea of ‘counterattitude’. It is pointed out that both expressed the idea of the analyst's unconscious as an ‘instrument’ for understanding the patient's unconscious. It follows that the decision to openly use or not to use countertransference in analysis also depends on the concept we have of it and on its extent. The psychoanalyst's real and illusory values and his convictions with regard to human nature influence the countertransference and the analytic relationship. Analytic listening itself may be distorted by it. We must be highly aware of this to avoid enclosing what the patient says in a theoretic scheme. What is needed, therefore, is an open theoretic scheme, more oriented towards understanding than interpretation. Aspects of analytic communication and of the relationship between language, thought and insight are examined. A humanistic point of view is assumed in distinguishing between the transferral and the real plane, and the reasons behind the legitimacy of such a distinction are expounded.



International Forum of Psychoanalysis11, 45-48, 2002

The Impossible Ideal: A Patient-Oriented Therapy

Marianne Horney Eckardt

Our profession is being challenged theoretically and by practical realities. Many of its basic premises are being questioned and a hostile managed care bureaucracy has been curtailing treatment opportunities. These challenges force a latent issue into full view. Is psychoanalytic wisdom tied to its dogma and technical rituals or can much of its wisdom be integrated into a more inclusive interdisciplinary perspective? Psychoanalysis has a history of resisting change. It defined too early what was and what was not to be considered psychoanalysis. Dogmatization made idols out of theories and the rituals of techniques. Theories are valuable tools only and not scientific truth. While institutes and official sanctions have lacked in open-mindedness, the unofficial practicing psychoanalyst has been far more creative in adapting psychoanalysis to the patient's needs and embracing the freedom to develop his or her idiosyncratic ways, wisdom, and skills. We need to increase our therapeutic repertoire beyond those that carry the label of psychoanalysis. I present some considerations that derive from my experience as a psychoanalytically trained dynamic psychotherapist.

God and the Unconscious

Rodney Bomford

Rodney Bomford

The Manor House, Modbury, Devon PL21 0RA. [email: bomford@mmodbury.fsnet.co.uk]

Rodney Bomford  

This paper summarizes the author's recent book, The Symmetry of God. It proposes that the concepts of God in the Christian tradition and of the Unconscious in Freudian theory have much in common. In particular, the mystics may be seen as explorers of the Unconscious and religious narrative as revelation of the Unconscious into Consciousness. Matte Blanco's theory about the logic of the Unconscious is used to support this. Theology has often turned to philosophy for ‘models’ of God and using the Unconscious as such opens discussion between spiritual and psychological understandings of humanity. While the traditional Christian language is retained, it is given a less objective feel than is customary, and religious truth is sharply distinguished from factual or empirical truth. This may make the language of faith more accessible to those who find literal interpretations incredible.

Introduction to ‘God and the Unconscious’

David Black

David Black

30 Cholmley Gardens, London NW6 1AG. [email: dmblack@clara.co.uk]

David Black  

We have spoken in the subtitle of this Conference of the New Dialogue between psychotherapy and religion. In a sense, we could have put that in an even larger context: the new dialogue between Science and Religion or, even larger yet, the new awareness of the social construction of facts and meanings. I shall introduce the Conference by speaking briefly about this wider context.

We can't read the classic texts of psychoanalysis now, including Freud's own writings on religion, without being aware how very much Freud belonged to the time of his formative years, the latter part of the nineteenth century. (He was 44 in 1900.) Freud's confidence in materialistic science, and his cheerful certainty that he personally had no need of what he called the fairytales of religion, are expressions of the Zeitgeist as much as they are anything personal to Freud himself. Indeed, there is something disappointingly shallow about much of Freud's account of religion. He didn't see, as his slightly older contemporary, Nietzsche, had seen, that the loss of religion, ‘the death of God’, as Nietzsche put it, would be a moral and social calamity, with literally incalculable consequences.

To appreciate the importance of events on this scale, we have to train ourselves to think in terms of several generations. Freud enjoyed calling himself a ‘godless Jew’, but he was the son of a religious Jew, and all his life he was in intense internal dialogue with his father. (Even at the age of 80, in the touching little paper entitled ‘A disturbance of memory on the Acropolis’ (Freud 1936), we see how vividly his father was still present to him.) The values of the godless psychoanalysis Freud created are in many ways strikingly similar to the values of traditional Judaism. And the internal worlds of ancestors are not tuned out after a single generation, as we become increasingly aware from working, for example, with descendants of Holocaust survivors.

‘God and the Unconscious’ took place at the Healing and Counselling Centre, St Marylebone Parish Church, London, in October 2000.

Is Empirical Research Compatible with Clinical Practice?

Christopher Clulow , Avi Shmueli , Christopher Vincent and Christopher Evans

Christopher Evans

The Tavistock Marital Studies Institute, The Tavistock Centre, 120 Belsize Lane, London NW3 5BA. [email: clulow@tmsi.org.uk]

The Tavistock and Portman Clinics NHS Trust, The Tavistock Centre, 120 Belsize Lane, London NW3 5BA. [email: cevans@tavi-port.org]

Christopher Evans  

This paper explores the provocative question in the title through the authors' experiences of working within a couple psychotherapy service. In it we hope to chart how it became possible to undertake empirical research in a clinical setting. Underlying the question we found a number of others. For example, when and how does empirical research threaten or enhance couples' therapies? Is empirical research a toxic introject, an idealized object and/or a real cultural, developmental experience for a clinical service? The process of change described in this paper involved conflict and took time to develop. We hope to demonstrate that what was achieved was done without detriment to the quality of the service offered and was not at the expense of those who used it. Our view is that the careful engagement we describe is most likely to have had a beneficial impact on both.

Chagall

John Birtchnell

John Birtchnell

London

John Birtchnell  

The persistent effort of so-called modern minds to explain mysteries … can yield nothing, in the long run, but the nostalgic satisfaction of the small boy who discovers at last that his mechanical duck was made up of two wheels, three springs and a screw. The little boy holds in his hands three springs, two wheels and a screw, objects which are doubtless reassuring, but he has lost his mechanical duck, and he has usually not found an explanation.

(Jean Anouilh)

There have always been two sides to me: the artist and the scientist. The artist wants to make art and the scientist wants to understand. At school I was torn between going to art school and going to medical school. Going to medical school won, but through medical school I continued to make art. In my final year at medical school (Birtchnell 1959) I wrote an article trying to explain what art was. It brought together the two sides of me. Some years into psychiatry, the conflict resurfaced in the form of: do I want to do psychotherapy or do I want to do research? Doing research won but I continued to do psychotherapy. The art side of me emerged as an interest in art therapy and, lately, I have treated a number of artists.

Artists often have serious psychological difficulties, and some commit suicide, but I do not believe that Chagall had serious psychological difficulties. The evidence suggests that he was a stable and well-balanced person. My reason for writing this article is my belief that what happens in art is sometimes similar to what happens in psychotherapy. The artist, like the person in psychotherapy, gives expression to ideas that are not understood. The artist, unselfconsciously and uncritically, allows the picture almost to paint itself, following the paint brush wherever it chooses to go, like the glass on an ouija board. Similarly, the psychoanalytic patient is encouraged to say whatever comes into her/his head, without question and without censor. Marian Milner (1987), who was as interested in art as she was in psychotherapy, used the term (borrowed from the reviewer of one of her books) the creative surrender, and struggled with the problem of how truly to trust ‘the unconscious’ (her quotation marks), in both herself and her patients. What fascinates me so about Chagall is the way that, unquestioningly, he was able to allow his imagery to flood out on to the canvas, and that he was probably quite unaware of, and, more importantly, uninterested in, where it was coming from. Howard Cooper

37 Lansdowne Road, London N3 1ET. [email: hcooper@waitrose.com]

Howard Cooper  

Both rabbis and therapists are on the receiving end of powerful projections, particularly the availability of their bodies as an object of phantasy. Both sets of professionals are seen as a potential source of healing and judgement, and both are viewed as having access to some hard-to-name yet sought-after power (God/the unconscious) - yet both are essentially storytellers. The analyst's stories about countertransference can illuminate the emotional communication between two people, but may perhaps need to retain some humility in the face of the mystery that we are so much more than our means to know give us to know.

Madness in Ancient Ireland

Brendan Mcmahon

Brendan Mcmahon

Temple House, Mill Hill Lane, Derby DE23 6SE

Brendan Mcmahon  

My purpose in this paper is to examine a number of traditional Irish narratives, whose primary concern is with psychosis, and to compare and contrast them with psychoanalytic narratives of the same phenomenon. While suggestive parallels are discovered, the Irish texts privilege phenomenology over aetiology, and emphasize the communal and interpersonal aspects of psychosis rather than the intrapersonal. These perspectives might usefully be incorporated into the psychoanalytic model.

‘Whose Handicap?’ Psychotherapy with People with Learning Disabilities

Mark Linington

Mark Linington

41 Brondesbury Road, London NW6 6BP. [email: mark@yarrowhousing.org.uk]

Mark Linington  

Whatever our disabilities might be, it is in our relationships that we become handicapped. A handicap is the consequence of a persistent failure to recognize who we are. We become handicapped when we are seen as something we are not, or when we are not seen at all. It is this process of not being seen, not being recognized as a different subject, which is illuminated by intersubjectivity theory:

Intersubjectivity theory postulates that the other must be recognized as another subject in order for the self to fully experience his or her subjectivity in the other's presence. This means, first, that we have a need for recognition and, second, a capacity to recognize others in return - mutual recognition. (Benjamin 1990, p. 186)

For babies born with a learning disability and their caregivers, this process of primary recognition and secondary mutual recognition can be profoundly disrupted. The meaning and impact of an infant with a learning disability are frequently an overwhelming experience for the parents. Given a lack of support from the world around them, the parents can dissociatively regulate their loss and terror, and the child with a learning disability becomes an absence (Stern et al. 1998a, p. 154):

With the news of a baby's problem, you can no longer clearly imagine this baby as a preschooler, an adolescent, an adult, as a parent, or as someone who could take care of you when you grow old. You've lost not only your ideal baby but, more important, the freedom to anticipate the future of your baby and your family.

As one mother said, I always imagined that one day I would be walking with my two children, holding each one by the hand. Now there is a gaping void in front of me. I don't know if I will have to spend my life taking care of an infant who could never walk. I don't know what will become of me.

Psychoanalysis at Its Limits: Navigating the Postmodern Turn edited by Anthony Elliott and Charles Spezzano. Published by Free Association Books, London, 1999; 306 Pages; £40.00 Hardback, £16.95 Paperback.

James Taylor

James Taylor

Leeds

James Taylor  

Last year, as we hit Harehills in search of curry, I rashly confessed my intention to review this book to an old, literary friend. His eyes twinkled in the drizzle as he replied, ‘You must be a sadomasochist’, and, to be fair, it seemed ‘cathexis’ of his target that evening was more imminent than mine! However, the ambivalence of his joke lingered as I read. I wondered whether my curiosity would stay the distance or whether my imagined endeavour would prove worthy of mockery. With hindsight, speculations as to whether I could come to terms with myself seem apt and congruent with this collection of quite thrilling essays in which several psychoanalysts attempt a similar thing. Their work depicts psychoanalysis circling around multiplicity, pluralism and ambivalence, somehow rediscovering itself through a refractive postmodern lens. Indeed it is one of the book's ironies that, to become reacquainted with Freud's dialectical vision, one has to journey with them, away from rather than via psychoanalytic convention. In contrast to the one-dimensional refutations which have failed to seriously confront the challenges of postmodernism, these writers can be seen to push their ideological and moral beliefs to the limit in sustained attempts to recast psychoanalysis in a contemporary light and, at points, to think the unthinkable. To this end, the thought of Freud, Klein, Winnicott, Bion, Lacan, Leowald, Heidigger and Foucault, in particular, is accessibly rehearsed and reconstructed into language which nonetheless meets the challenges of complexity.

In Chapter 1, Elliott and Spezzano cast psychoanalysis and postmodernism in symbiotic play, developing an analysis of how one encounters the other in diverse contexts. Following an exploration of conflicting notions of modernism and postmodernism, they suggest that there are ‘three faces of postmodernism’: the aesthetic, the social-theoretic and philosophical, and the private and intersubjective. Aided by this more differentiated backdrop, they critically examine recent psychoanalytic critiques of postmodern theorizing arguing that ‘the postmodern turn’ in contemporary psychoanalysis has on the whole been poorly conceptualized. They instead suggest the potential for lively, dynamic discourse between these overlapping areas of thought by producing hypotheses about the nature of human subjectivity, psychic fragmentation and dislocation, and the realms of representation and signification. Throughout I felt thirsty for clinical vignettes to join with their thought but, equally, I was impressed by their depressive humour and humility, particularly given the scope of the task in hand. In Chapter 2, Jane Flax masterfully draws on Foucault's work to address the question of whether psychoanalysis can survive in the postmodern West.

Evaluation of Outcome in A Dynamically Orientated Group for Adult Males Who Have Been Sexually Abused in Childhood

Audrey Morrison and Linda Treliving

Linda Treliving

1 Edward Street, Dundee DD2 5NS

Linda Treliving  

At a time when males abused in childhood are coming increasingly to attention of clinical services, we review the literature, describe the process and report on clinical outcomes of a slow open long-term dynamically orientated group for abused adult males. Twenty-nine men referred to the local psychotherapy service for consideration for inclusion in the group are discussed along with some of the most prevailing themes, namely identification with the aggressor, self-esteem, guilt and sexuality. Symptoms were measured using the SCL 90-R and demonstrate relatively high levels of psychological distress in this group at initial assessment. There is significant improvement in global scores, interpersonal sensitivity, depression and psychoticism in the group of 13 men who engaged in therapy for at least six months compared with those who did not.

The authors conclude that symptom measurement provides evidence that group psychotherapy is a useful therapeutic approach in a group of men who might otherwise be considered unsuitable for psychotherapeutic interventions due to symptom severity and personality difficulties.

Tessa Baradon  

This is a vividly presented session of work with a highly complex case, involving emotional and physical violence between mother and child. In a situation of heightened and volatile emotions it is often difficult for the therapist to think, and the behavioural enactments force the therapist to act on the spot. The material raises questions regarding therapeutic frames of reference, the choice of technique in intervention, and the patients' experiences of the therapist in the transference and as a ‘developmental object’.

The referral was made because of Owen's ‘violent and disruptive behaviour’, particularly towards his mother and sister. The background information contextualizes the referral: Owen was exposed to violence in his parents' relationship in his first year, and he and his mother are now engaged in a mutually violent relationship, to which 8-week-old Susan is exposed. Thus we are alerted to the intergenerational repetition of interactions characterized by violence and terror. In infancy such relationships constitute trauma to the developing neuropsychological structures (Schore 2001).

The session contains enactments of all the above elements - violence, terror and trauma. Owen quickly presents this to the therapist through his hurt lip. He may also be expressing the family's hope that this is a place for ‘hurts’. Ms S's explanation of Owen's hurt lip immediately introduces her attributions and recriminations. Mother repudiates the therapist's attempts to explain Owen's behaviour (getting into a state and biting) in terms of mental states (because he was anxious about Susan's injection). She blames her children for her state of depletion (‘worn out’ by the sleepless nights). Owen tries to ‘interrupt’ - stop - his mother's thrusting anger. This is the here-and-now of attack and fear in their relationship. The therapist tries again to modify mother's negative attributions (of aggressive intent) by representing Owen's internal world - linking his wakefulness with his anxiety over his destructiveness.

This description of a 3-year-old boy out of the control of his mother who feels helpless and hopeless is a familiar experience to those who work with parents and children under five. On this occasion there is a single mother with a history of unsatisfactory relationships with violent and now absent men. The small boy seems to take the place of the absent man and provide a relationship which feels like a substitute and a repetition. In this description his mother keeps telling the therapist about his excitement with ‘blood and gore’. There is a need on the mother's part to get the therapist to understand the importance of this and it dominates her communication for some time at the beginning of the session. How can one intervene effectively in this relationship which is so dominating mother and child and where the violence is projected back and forth between them?

The first issue is to engage them and the therapist has succeeded in doing this; this is the second session. It is necessary for the mother to feel supported by the therapist and the structure of the meeting, and it is clear in this second meeting that she does feel helped. She, with the therapist's help, is better able to control Owen, which she acknowledges in this session. An important part of this engagement comes from the mother's feeling that her concerns are listened to and accepted. She repeats several times the descriptions of Owen's excitement in upsetting her and his enjoyment of destructiveness, and it may be that in the earlier part of the session she is not sure whether this is being heard. The therapist is trying to make a link with Owen directly and this seems to cause the mother to become competitive for the therapist's attention.

A Personal View of A Conference Held in Memory of Stephen Mitchell

Marguerite Valentine PHD

Marguerite Valentine

39 Womersley Road, London N8 9AP. [email: margvalentine@hotmail.com]

Marguerite Valentine  

Those of us familiar with the work of Stephen Mitchell (1993, 1995, 1997) who died tragically and suddenly in December 2000, looked forward with some anticipation to attending the first Conference for the International Association for Relational Psychoanalysis and Psychotherapy in New York City on 18-20 January 2002. Stephen Mitchell has done much to critique traditional psychoanalytic theory and technique, and from this has developed a contemporary theoretical and clinical practice. As part of a small British contingent, it was inspirational to mix with 1200 like-minded colleagues, some of whom came from as far away as Australia.

The remit? To develop our thinking and knowledge of the Relational School of Analysis, as exemplified by a growing number of analytic writers and clinicians. The Conference, entitled ‘Sense and Sensibility’, elaborated this theme with special attention focused on the development of a narrative, during the process of what might be called ‘a sustained empathic inquiry’. As one speaker commented, ‘No stories, no self’. To practise in this way the analyst moves from a ‘neutral’ position to an ‘active’ one, along the lines that Ferenczi wrote about.

Hence there is a shift from an analysis of the intra-personal towards the inter-subjective, making use of the mutuality of the relationship between the analyst and the patient. A consideration of the ‘real’ experience in terms of the patient's history also takes centre stage, and how the original trauma becomes enacted within the consulting room. With the opportunity for opening a new dialogue comes the possibility of repair, as both patient and analyst work with their own and the other's transference and countertransference. This way of working, by implication, confronts the present power relationship, whereby there is an assumption that the analyst knows more, and the patient less. Interpretations are more likely to be seen as hypotheses, rather than ‘ex cathedra’ statements reflecting the analyst's ideological beliefs.

Kleinians: Psychoanalysis Inside Out is about the lives and work of Klein, Susan Isaacs, Joan Riviere, Adrian Stokes, Herbert Rosenfeld, Wilfred Bion, Esther Bick, Frances Tustin, Hanna Segal and Ronald Britton, eminent members of the Kleinian Group of the British Psycho-Analytical Society. Adrian Stokes was not a clinician, but his writing on art and literature has been greatly influenced by Klein.

Each chapter, one for each author, stands in its own right and each one can be read quite separately. The author has done an impressive amount of work in collecting information about these ten remarkable people and in selecting the essentials of their writing. As a result she gives an interesting account of their work within a biographical context. Although some who have known these authors in person or who have studied their work in depth could feel that Janet Sayers provides a rather superficial picture, they will all the same be enriched by her work. To think simultaneously of the person and the work of ten leading authors is a considerable achievement, which cannot fail to impress the reader.

Different stories, different backgrounds but all extraordinarily original and creative in their study of the human mind. The magnitude of the task leads, at times, to quantity rather than quality prevailing. As a consequence, the personalities in question can become flattened in the process and the accuracy of the original formulation lost. It is impossible to miss, for example, the potential contradiction between the assertion that Miss Bick seems to have had ‘a happy infancy’ and, in the next paragraph, the extraordinary list of losses which occurred during the first five years of her life!

Case-studies are the most significant aspect of the book, particularly as they are told in the chronological context of the authors' lives. Compared with the general light-hearted style of the book, case-studies make intense, demanding reading. The author uses almost verbatim material from the original source, as in the cases of Rosenfeld and Bion.

On the cover of both books is a picture by Marc Chagall. It is a self-portrait painted in 1922. On his head is a drawing of a simple house, home. A couple, dressed in the clothes we recognize as those worn by Jews of that era, walk together in the foreground. To their left is a young woman with a baby in her arms. Perhaps it describes something of the central topic in these books. Is it possible to carry the past and meet the future in a creative way, and what might contribute to such an outcome? It is this very general question that seems to be at the heart of the these books, set as they both are in a period of the utmost horror and devastation, the Nazi uprising and persecution and the Second World War.

The first book It Is a New Kind of Diaspora is about the migration of psychoanalysts fleeing from Europe, leaving behind both their geographical and psychoanalytic homes, and the factors which determined their fate in the host countries. This is what Anna Freud referred to as ‘a new kind of diaspora’. The second book, just as the title says, is about ‘tradition, change and creativity’. The tradition is Freudian psychoanalysis, the change is Melanie Klein's new and innovative ideas, and then the book considers how it came about that there was a creative outcome.

Steiner's interest is in the legacy of Freud's work and he brings to these issues a breadth of knowledge of history, language, religion, psychoanalysis and epistemology that is daunting. He is also one of the the archivists for the British Psychoanalytical Society which has given him a particular opportunity to study documents relevant to these issues.

Jean Arundale  

IN THIS ISSUE …

For analyses that get stuck or reach impasse, new theoretical input is helpful. Richard Carvalho offers an alternative view to Steiner's psychic retreat in which the issue is not defences against primitive aggression but rather an overwhelming fear of uncontained affect due to attachment failures from the past. After linking in the ideas of Ferrari and Matte Blanco, Carvalho discusses the technical implications of these considerations in relation to some of the clinical material from Steiner's (2000) paper, ‘Containment, enactment and communication’.

Patients with a sense of entitlement are often encountered in clinical practice. Jackie Gerrard explores this topic, taking as her starting point Freud's paper ‘The Exceptions’ and bringing in the ideas of Rosenfeld, Kohut, Britton, Mollon and Main. She differentiates between the underlying configurations of narcissistic injury, deprivation and privation, with implications for technique.

In Ibsen's Peer Gynt trolls become human beings by finding themselves through being loved.

Irene Freeden gives excerpts from the analyses of two female patients showing their struggles and transformations, using the concept of the Claustrum espoused by Meltzer and Bion's ideas of alpha function, Love, Hate and Knowledge to illustrate psychopathology and what did and didn't change.

Successive intermittent psychotherapy over the patient's life-span is already practised in our profession, as pointed out by Gertrud Mander, who goes on to propose an appropriate brief therapy in which free association gives way to active focusing on the central dynamic conflict. She cites the work of Mann, Balint, Malan, Luborsky and Stern. After current therapeutic goals are reached the patient then has the opportunity to return later when new crises occur, thus shortening the therapy contract.

The supervision group is widely used in the training of psychodynamic counsellors and psychotherapists. Christopher Scanlon writes of the group dynamics that help or hinder the learning process, incorporating knowledge gleaned from the field of professional education and using the language of reflective practice. Thus, a culture of inquiry is created relevant to CPD.

From Free Association to the Dynamic Focus: Towards A Model of Recurrent Psychotherapy

Gertrud Mander

Gertrud Mander

24 Chalcot Crescent, London NW1 8YD. [email: g.mander@virgin.net]

Gertrud Mander  

This paper sets out to describe some of the recent changes in psychotherapy in terms of the needs of new clinical populations. Written from the perspective of the brief therapist it is about new treatment approaches in various clinical contexts which are setting time-limits and advocate focusing on selected material, in order to shorten working contracts. The history of brief focal psychotherapy is charted from the first attempt set up at the Tavistock Clinic by the analysts Balint and Malan, to the theories of Mann, Sifneos, Luborsky and, most recently, Daniel Stern who advocates ‘reapplications of treatment’ as did Freud and Erikson, i.e. ‘a form of serial life-span therapy which is the continuation of a single treatment across discontinuities in a life-span’. It emphasizes the importance of careful assessment at the outset of treatment, in order to find the ‘nuclear conflict’ (French), the ‘point of maximum pain’ (Hinshelwood) or the ‘therapeutic metaphor’ (Stern) which will constitute their chosen dynamic focus, as well as to formulate a justification for the therapist's amending of the time-frame, for the adoption of an active stance and for modifications of technique to achieve the therapeutic goal. Thus the aim of ‘making a significant difference’ in the client's self-perception and functioning substitutes for the structural changes aimed for in long-term therapy. Some clinical vignettes attempt to show how this can be done. Finally, there is the plea for an acceptance of ‘recurrent psychotherapy’ which in reality is already practised widely: more and more patients are receiving successive therapy contracts in the course of their lives, returning for more therapy whenever they encounter a fresh disabling crisis.

Brett Kahr  

In 1925, Sigmund Freud became the very first psychoanalyst to publish a professional autobiography, the famous Selbstdarstellung (An Autobiographical Study). Since that time, quite a considerable number of first, second, and third generation colleagues and disciples followed suit with their own more or less revealing autobiographical offerings, notably those by Franz Alexander, Leopold Bellak, Wilfred Bion, Helene Deutsch, Michael Fordham, Roy Grinker, Ernest Jones, Carl Gustav Jung, Ronald Laing, Margaret Little, Margaret Mahler, Jules Masserman, Esther Menaker, Karl Menninger, Sándor Radó, Wilhelm Reich, Theodor Reik, Wilhelm Stekel and Fritz Wittels - all published in the last half-century - with some as yet unpublished sketches by the formidable triumvirate of Melanie Klein, Clifford Scott and Donald Winnicott waiting in the wings.

Although the early psychoanalysts leapt into print with autobiographical gusto, perhaps because of their historical proximity to Freud, or as ambassadors of a new profession, later generations of clinicians have usually failed to do so. Of the 23 individuals listed above, only Dr Ronald D. Laing began his training after 1950. Apart from Laing, one would be hard pressed to find more recent professional autobiographies in the field of psychoanalysis. Perhaps this results from a greater triumph over narcissistic, exhibitionistic displays among more recently trained practitioners, or maybe modern workers have become more sensitive to the potentially adverse consequences of so much brazen self-revelation. To play devil's advocate, it may be that more recent, bourgeoisified, technocratized clinicians have very little to say, unlike our more revolutionary, pioneering forebears.

Amid this climate of relative silence about the detailed life-histories of more recently trained psychoanalysts, one greets with great relish the exquisitely well-styled professional autobiography of Professor John Gedo, arguably the most polemical graduate of the Chicago Institute for Psychoanalysis, and almost the most prolific (with the certain exception of Professor Thomas Szasz), a man whose literary corpus outstripped that of his sometime teacher, the late Dr Heinz Kohut, in terms of sheer numbers of published books and essays.

The much loved psychoanalyst Pearl King occupies a unique place in the hearts and minds of thousands of mental health professionals both here in Great Britain and abroad. A practising psychoanalyst for over 51 years, Miss

263

King has trained and supervised such a large proportion of the leading figures in British psychoanalysis and psychotherapy that it would be virtually impossible to quantify her influence on contemporary clinical psychotherapy.

Pearl King's multitudinous achievements deserve to be commemorated in monograph form, for she has contributed substantially to so many arenas within the field of psychoanalysis. A pioneering industrial psychologist in the 1940s, eager to improve the quality of life for members of the work-force, Miss King trained as a psychoanalyst, having chosen Dr John Rickman as her Training Analyst. Since qualification from the Institute of Psycho-Analysis in 1951, King has laboured tirelessly to promote the cause of psychoanalysis, both within the British Psycho-Analytical Society (serving as Deputy President to both Dr Wilfred Bion and Dr Donald Winnicott, and then years later as the first ever non-medical President), but also as Honorary Secretary to the International Psycho-Analytical Association.

Renowned for her frequently cited and path-breaking publications on analytical technique, and on the treatment of the older patient, amongst many other topics, King may be perhaps best known for her gargantuan contribution to the history of psychoanalysis. This includes her editorial work on the collected papers of John Rickman (1957), her joint editorship of the infamous ‘Controversial Discussions’ (King & Steiner 1991), and especially her impassioned creation of the Archives of the British Psycho-Analytical Society, a lovingly maintained repository for unpublished historical documents which has served as the role model for many other archives world-wide. Without recourse to the Archives established by Pearl King, many an historical text would be grossly impoverished.

Andrea Sabbadini

Andrea Sabbadini  

When Hugh Brody's Nineteen Nineteen was released in 1985, film-critic Philip French, comparing it with three classic films on psychoanalysis (Pabst's Geheimnisse einer Seele, Hitchcock's Spellbound and Huston's Freud) wrote in his review that ‘with Nineteen Nineteen the cinema has at last reached some maturity in its approach to Freud, psychoanalysis and their place in history’ (French 1985). Before discussing Brody's film, I would like to show how those three movies mentioned by French - which belong to a small, yet to us important, sub-genre of feature films - intended to represent, though in some respects end up misrepresenting, our profession.

Aesthetically located somewhere between the claustrophobic expressionistic world of ‘Kammerspiel’ and the emergence of the ‘Neue Sachlichkeit’ of Georg Wilhelm Pabst's best work, his Geheimnisse einer Seele (Secrets of a Soul) (1926) is an experimental project intended to introduce the general audience to a psychoanalytical understanding of mental phenomena and to their peculiar idiom, in a thought-provoking and visually engaging form. The film describes the mid-life identity crisis of a sexually impotent chemist (played by Werner Krauss, who had been the Doppelgänger mad psychiatrist in Das Kabinett des Dr Caligari, 1919). He becomes obsessed with knives and the conflictual desire to kill his beloved wife, of whose relationship with a cousin, visiting from abroad, he feels jealous. A chance meeting with a psychoanalyst, driving him to his couch and to the exploration of a frightening dream, eventually resolves his deep-rooted, oedipally-coloured neurosis. Geheimnisse einer Seele is filled with simplistic generalizations and a manneristic use of symbolism: blades (which sever links and create new boundaries), a key, a doll, mirrors (which fix identities and confound the self), a phallic tower. Interestingly, symbolism was also a trademark of the Surrealist movement that in those years was producing analytically-inspired films, such as Buñuel's Un Chien Andalou (1928).

I would like to begin by expressing my gratitude to the clinician contributing the material, for the opportunity to think about such an interesting, difficult session and to be able to discuss it. It gives us an excellent chance to look at the possible causes of violence in children such as these, as well as to reflect on issues of theory and technique surrounding our work with very young children and their parents. This session presents us with an opportunity to see how the work with both the adult and the very young child involved in this sort of therapeutic situation, restricted by its brevity, takes place simultaneously. I say this because I understand the therapist's interventions throughout the session as having a dual purpose: to contain the child's escalating rage and destructiveness and to attempt to explain it to the mother in such a way as to improve, or perhaps create, her capacity to understand her child's behaviour and, through that understanding, enable her to handle it in a more satisfactory and productive manner.

Containing the child's aggression becomes a major feature in Owen's case because, as Anna Freud often reminded us, acting out that does not lead to insight or to change and for which interpretation is not accepted is, of course, not beneficial.

The way in which one talks to such very young children is influenced by some of the main difficulties encountered in such work: the limitations imposed by their capacity to understand what is being said to them, their lack of insight into their abnormalities, the absence of a therapeutic alliance, the immaturity of their ego and, most important of all, the reality that the child's dependency on his parents reduces the possibility of his developing a fully fledged transference to the therapist. This is all very relevant because it colours the way in which one addresses a child.

(Harry, he's here to help (Harry, un ami qui vous veut du bien), Director: Dominik Moll, Distributor: Boomerang Pictures)

Melanie Klein's descriptions of primitive defences have been brought to life in this remarkable French film written by Dominik Moll and Gilles Marchand and directed by Dominik Moll. Winner of 4 Cesar Awards in 2001, it is a mystery thriller in the Hitchcockian tradition but with what seems to be a very ambiguous moral message. It is also more if you care to take a closer look. Rather it would be more correct to say: if you care to take a step back and assume an analytical stance. Primitive defences such as projective identification are like that. Move too close and you get swallowed up without realizing what is happening to you, but move too far away and you won't have a clue what's going on. In a very subtle yet, at the same time, terrifying way, we are shown how the defence mechanisms of splitting and projective identification can drain the personality of much instinctual energy, restricting sexual and aggressive drives and, with them, many creative elements. It shows how one may be ready to compromise and accept this situation rather than face the sometimes overwhelming anxiety involved in recuperating these elements which are felt to be much too threatening to the ego. Despite the very down to earth, realistic beginning of the film where external reality dominates, we slowly enter, without realizing it at first, into a more surreal world, the inner world of Michel, the main character of the film. Slowly and eerily, fantasy becomes reality but the audience, like Michel, is at first naïve, unaware of what is happening.

Michel is a French teacher. He has an attractive, understanding wife, Claire, and they are the parents of three small girls. They are worn out by the small but innumerable problems of everyday life. Michel is a ‘nice guy’, a man of compromise who tries to accommodate everyone in order to avoid conflict. A young man with much patience. Or is he? What is the price he has paid for his ‘normal/neurotic’ appearance? Suddenly, Harry appears on the scene. Harry is travelling with his fiancée, Plum (‘bébé’), and they invite themselves for a visit. In fact Michel has no recollection at all of Harry, but Harry seems to know and remember a lot about Michel. He recounts that Michel was reputed to be a great lover and also tells of how Michel used to write for the school newspaper. Harry remembers every story and poem. He even knows one of the poems off by heart which he recites to Michel and his wife one evening. It is about a long knife covered by a ‘skin of darkness’.

This paper describes an individual psychotherapy conducted in Urdu by a psychoanalytic psychotherapist in training, using Hobson's Conversational Model of therapy. This integrational approach draws upon an eclectic range of thought including psychoanalysis, philosophy, cognitive therapy, systems theory, particular schools of philosophy and the Romantic Movement. An outline of the background issues leading to this particular case-study is followed by a case description emphasizing particular aspects of the therapeutic endeavour that allowed creative change and conflict resolution to occur, including the flexibility and openness of the therapist's stance.
