This paper argues that a potent cause of impasse in analysis/psychotherapy is the fear of annihilation by uncontained affect, and that the ‘retreat’ (Steiner 1993) to which the patient has recourse is often prompted by such anxiety rather than by paranoid-schizoid or depressive anxiety. Such retreats are marked by defensive attempts to occupy the object, to abolish separation, and to avoid emotional links that are feared will bring on the overwhelming affect related to attachment failures from the past. Thus, analysis itself is perceived unconsciously to be the disaster against which the patient is likely to implement an impasse. This approach offers an alternative to the concept of retreat as described by Steiner (Steiner 1993), but is not intended to replace it. Either model may be indicated clinically in different circumstances. The author introduces the theories of Armando Ferrari and Ignacio Matte Blanco, both consonant with Ogden's theory of the autistic-contiguous position and offering alternative explanations for the clinical phenomena. The technical implications of these considerations are then discussed in relation to some of the clinical material from Steiner's (2000) paper, ‘Containment, enactment and communication’.

I take clinical material from a nine-month period in a slow open analytic psychotherapy group for mothers and babies, to illustrate its potential as a therapeutic modality. I describe the process of creating a reliable setting, or ‘group culture’, and its role as a prerequisite for therapeutic change. Vignettes are used, alongside my commentary, to display the passionate involvement between mothers and infants, also with therapists, which develops in a shared therapeutic experience. Fakhry Davids  

The events of September 11th were brought home to us all by wall-to-wall television coverage of airliners crashing into the twin towers like giant guided missiles, followed moments later by the towers collapsing into heaps of rubble. These were awful, shocking images of devastation on a scale that was quite simply unbearable. It is one thing to think ‘It's just like a scene from a Hollywood disaster movie!’, but how can you take in the fact that there, in front of you, a jet full of people is ploughing straight into offices also full of ordinary people? And that the explosion, flames and smoke you see speak of people being burnt and suffocated to an unimaginable death at that very moment? And, in the sequence showing the collapse of the towers, you were watching perhaps thousands of people being crushed to death under tons of shattered glass, mangled steel and broken concrete? And the chilling realization that those tiny specks hurtling down beside the towers, moments before their collapse, were real people jumping to certain death a hundred floors below - a death that must have felt preferable to an infinitely more terrible and horrifying fate inside. For all of us living in the West, here was a human catastrophe that we could not keep at an emotional distance - it was all too obvious that there but for the grace of God go you or I.

As psychoanalysts we know that psychically unbearable events call into play powerful defences whose aim is to protect us from perceived danger. To the normal mind, racist modes of thinking1 constitute the most readily available constellation of such defences, and these have been evident from the very outset. Early that afternoon a close friend rang, deeply distressed that ‘They say Muslims have done it’, terrified that they were about to bomb Pakistan (where she has relatives), and desperately praying that, like the Oklahoma bombing, this would turn out to be another home-grown attack. The following day a patient addressed this same issue from the opposite end. He hoped that the victims under the rubble would turn out to represent every colour, race, creed and nationality of the human family, thus giving the lie to any simplistic notion that it was an attack by ‘them’ on ‘us’.

Uncle Petros and Goldbach's Conjecture by Apostolos Doxiadis. Published by Faber and Faber, London, 2000; 209 pages; £9.99 paperback.

Joseph Schwartz

Joseph Schwartz

London

Joseph Schwartz  

In a little gem of a novel, Doxiadis spins a tale of Uncle Petros, an unknown mathematician of genius, who devotes his life to the most famous unsolved problem in Western mathematics. Told in a beautifully spare style from the

442

retrospective viewpoint of a nephew who had aspired to be a mathematician just like his uncle, a black sheep in the family, we encounter the fascinating culture, accurately limned, of world-class mathematics in the twentieth-century. We meet the Cambridge mathematical superstars, G.H. Hardy and J.E. Littlewood, their colleague, the legendary number theorist Srinivasa Ramanujan and, across the water, the fabulous eccentricity of Kurt Goedel and the denizens of the Institute for Advanced Study at Princeton.

And, of course, we are treated to a charming encounter with Christian Goldbach's famous conjecture of 1742. In the words of epitaph on Uncle Petros's grave:

Every Even Number Greater than 2 is the Sum of Two Primes

Along the way we find ourselves engaged with the anxieties and passions of the lives of our mathematical brothers and sisters from Goedel's terrifying incompleteness theorem to the pathological competitive stress endemic to professional mathematics. Doxiadis knows whereof he speaks and, like Primo Levi with industrial chemistry, has created literature from the materials of a marginalized corner of human experience.

Doxiadis has written a poignant meditation on the pain of human failure in the face of an impossible task. But there is another level to his story as well. I believe that Doxiadis's own youthful involvement with mathematics has informed his imagination in a way that makes him move beyond a spare appreciation of the pain of human hubris. At another level he succeeds, in the way he ends his tale, in evoking in us the feeling of what it is like to be seduced by the tension and excitement of a complex mathematical problem. We get a glimpse, perhaps the very glimpse that Doxiadis himself might have had, of a possible way to prove or disprove Goldbach's conjecture. Keeping within the bounds of his fable Doxiadis leaves us with the thrill of what it might actually feel like to do mathematics at the very highest level of achievement.

Melanie Klein: Her Work in Context by Meira Likierman. Published by Continuum, London and New York, 2001; 202 pages; £16.99.

Victoria Davenport

Victoria Davenport

London

Victoria Davenport  

This is an important book that's in danger of being overlooked, mainly due to a nondescript title, predictable cover (the usual portrait of Klein), and a quote by Adam Phillips, all of which do little to convey its true value. It isn't, however, just another book on Klein as it contains valuable insights by someone who can not only write and isn't boring, but who will convince the most rabid non-Kleinian that Mrs Klein wasn't all bad.

My heart did sink a bit while reading the Introduction, fearing I was in for 200 pages of adulation, but I soon realized that, while clearly supporting Klein, the author is also very willing to look critically at her key papers. Although I'm sure some of the interpretations will provoke discussion, I didn't sense that the reader is being asked to discard previously held ideas, pro or con, but rather to consider another point of view, as well as learning a great deal about the ‘context’ in which Mrs Klein worked, both theoretically and politically.

I came across by chance Likierman's 1993 paper ‘Primitive object love in Melanie Klein's thinking: early theoretical influences’ (an interesting paper, and a good reason to have a bibliography - where is it?), which discusses how it came about that Klein's work was interpreted as being primarily about aggression and destructive forces. This book is a continuation of that theme, with a similar historical/theoretical slant. Here, the author explains that at the time of presentation Klein's material was shocking partly because no one before had dared to speak so openly about aggression and the infant psyche, although Freud had broken the ice with the essays on sexuality:

Klein paints a picture of childhood sadism that is unprecedented in its ferocity, and that seems out of keeping with ordinary expectations. The picture is so stark that it has created, then and since, an unfortunate reputation for her theory. (p. 48)

As Likierman points out, however, it wasn't the sexual material that was difficult for Klein's colleagues, but having to get their heads round the concept of unconscious phantasy.

Jackie Gerrard  

He never wants anything but what's right and fair; only when you come to settle what's right and fair, it's everything that he wants and nothing that you want. And that's his idea of compromise.

(Thomas Hughes Tom Brown's Schooldays, Pt. II, Ch. 2)

Patients with problems of entitlement experience themselves as undernourished while the therapist experiences them as insatiable.

(Tenzer 1987, p. 270)

These quotations illustrating ‘a sense of entitlement’ are, I feel sure, recognizable to us all. Patients such as these consider themselves to be especially entitled, with special rights and privileges. Many analysts in the USA were engaged in writing on a sense of entitlement in the late 1980s (Billow 1999; Blechner 1987; Bromberg 1983; Grey 1987; Grotstein 1990; Moses & Moses-Hrushovski 1990; Rothstein 1977, 1979; Tenzer 1987). Moses and Moses-Hrushovski (1990) suggest three categories in attitudes of entitlement - normal, excessive and restricted. Normal is related to that which is reality-orientated, i.e. correctly assessing that to which one is legitimately entitled. My focus in this paper is not on the normal sense of entitlement but on the two polarized extremes - either excessive, with considerable narcissism and grandiosity, or restricted, which they say is often a reaction formation where the patient is found to function in a modest and self-denying way (see also Jacobson 1959). Not surprisingly, we find that these are two sides of the same coin and one masks the other. As Moses and Moses-Hrushovski state, ‘narcissistic overvaluation and grandiosity often are accompanied by a strong undervaluation, a strong sense of worthlessness or impotence’ (1990, p. 69).

Many American theorists have taken as their starting point, Freud's (1916) paper, ‘Some character types met with in psychoanalytic work’, where Freud refers to the ‘Exceptions’, patients who express their sense of ‘deserving’ or of having suffered.

Fantasy and Imagination in Winnicott's Work

Richard Frankel PHD

Richard Frankel

113 Belmont Street, Belmont, MA 02178, USA. [email: rfrankl@ix.netcom.com]

Richard Frankel  

Introduction

In this paper, I will explore Winnicott's approach to fantasy, imagination and the therapeutic engagement of fantasy-images. Winnicott's case accounts, with both children and adults, bear testimony to his unique understanding of the processes of fantasy, as evidenced by his detailed descriptions of the emergence and unfolding of fantasy-images in the context of the dialogical exchange between analyst and patient. In his theoretical papers on transitional objects, potential space, and the role of fantasy in psychic development, a philosophy of the imagination implicitly emerges for Winnicott that is heedful of Freud's caution in relation to the productions of fantasy, yet at the same time places great value on the phenomenological integrity of fantasy-images, thus calling into question primary psychoanalytic assumptions about the role of fantasy and imagination in psychological life.

The paper is divided into two parts. In Part One, I will examine the key theoretical ideas that give ground to an emerging theory of fantasy and image in Winnicott's work. In Part Two, I will examine a therapeutic consultation with a very young child, the Piggle, in which we explore the particularities of Winnicott's approach to engaging images in the context of an ongoing treatment. By elucidating the links between his theoretical insights into the relationship between fantasy, imagination and reality and his actual work with fantasy-images in the course of treatment, the aim of this paper is to show the distinct contribution Winnicott makes toward a psychoanalytic theory of the image.

‘In My End is My Beginning’: T.S. Eliot'S The Waste Land and after

Paul Schimmel

Paul Schimmel

PO Box 37, Roseville, NSW 2069, Australia

Paul Schimmel  

The publication of The Waste Land established Eliot's reputation as a major poet. The poem was written out of an experience of emotional ‘breakdown’, and its innovative free associative form conveys a sense of psychological fragmentation. While Eliot emphasized the necessary distance that must be achieved between personal experience and successful creative expression, all his major poems were written out of periods of personal crisis and growth, and remain intensely personal. This paper explores links between Eliot's personal emotional experience and the poetry. It suggests that for Eliot poetry was part of a journey of self-exploration and, at the time of The Waste Land and subsequently, became a vital part of his struggle towards a new integration within his self.

Miranda Davies  

I have chosen to look at the way that the session illustrates the operation of Fordham's model of the deintegration and reintegration of the self in relation to discoveries in neuroscience. The session itself seems to me to be exemplary, a model of family work with under fives. I was deeply impressed by the way that the therapist could interpret Owen's need for mind to mind contact with his mother, his jealousy and attacks on the mother-therapist couple, his regression, his omnipotence, the guilt and anxiety underlying his violence, his oedipal confusion and his need to effect normal splitting between good and bad; and all this in the midst of his mother's distressed talking and Owen's frighteningly violent behaviour.

The finding that the development of the brain and, consequently, the development of the mind are ‘experience dependent’, operates in analytical psychology as corroboration of Fordham's model of the self. In his ‘Notes for the formation of a model of infant development’, he writes about how he sought to define the primary state of the self, based on Jung's proposition that the self is the totality of the personality, mind and body, whose goal is individuation.

When I did so I had to recognize that [the primary self] cannot be experienced - it has no features that can be experienced; but like DNA it unfolds when brought into relation with a suitable environment producing matter which can be perceived and experienced emotionally and mentally - the two classes of experience are not to be separated in the first place. It is from these subjective and objective data that the self is inferred; I conceived it to be a psychosomatic entity containing within it the inherited potential for forming the experience of a body and a psyche. This entity is bounded at first by a cell membrane and later by a skin. (Fordham 1993, p. 6)

Fordham saw the infant's self as separate from the mother, and in order to express the dynamic by which the self comes into relation to her he used the term ‘deintegration’. Deintegration is the unfolding of the self towards a new experience, with its concomitant activity and affect. It is followed by quiet states in which the new experience is taken in and assimilated, which he called ‘reintegration’. Fordham refers to his hypothesis as being useful and doing the job of holding data together (p. 6).

Chains of Eros: The Sexual in Psychoanalysis by André Green. Published by Rebus Press, London, 2000; 238 pages.

David Mann

David Mann

London and Tunbridge Wells

David Mann  

This book is a further development of Green's ideas encouraging psychoanalysis to refocus on its origins and the centrality of the erotic. The sexual was always the cornerstone in Freud's thinking. As Green states, the importance of the sexual is: (1) its capacity to form connections in diverse registers, including the non-sexual, which demonstrates the extent of its power; (2) the sexual is transgressive, crosses limits and leaves its mark in those areas it has infiltrated; (3) the contours of the sexual are ‘endlessly varied’. (I would personally be more tentative here and say almost endlessly varied.)

Green draws our attention to the developments in sexuality since Freud and remarks that, during the twentieth century, more changes have taken place in the domain of sexuality than in all previous aeons. The developments in sexuality in the culture at large have had a paradoxical impact on psychoanalysis during the twentieth century, where Freud's inheritors have reduced the importance of the sexual in psychoanalysis. Green proposes that the Puritanism that lost ground to Freud took revenge on the founding father by getting the better of his successors. These ‘new Puritans’ include Klein and Winnicott and their followers. He is particularly critical of the Kleinian tradition in which the penis is reduced to merely being the successor of the nipple, and sexuality reliant on the feeding qualities of introjection and incorporation. Green wryly but accurately notes that the vagina, therefore, becomes little more than a nether mouth and the penis a nether nipple: ‘One could almost state that, for the Kleinians, the complete model of genital satisfaction is nothing other than fellatio!’ (p. 18).

The main focus of the book is an examination of sexuality in the psyche. Sexuality is a process which originates in and sets off from the body to the object, but also moves from the object to the depths of the body.

A Troll in the Consulting Room

Irene Freeden

Irene Freeden

104 Kingston Road, Oxford OX2 6RN

Irene Freeden  

Taking Ibsen's tale of Peer Gynt as a framework, this paper presents an account of the psychotherapy of two patients. The first, a beautiful young woman, initially profoundly distressed, frightened and confused, who found the pressure of her studies overwhelming, has been enabled through her treatment to lead a successful academic and social life. However, the psychopathic nature of her relationship to objects has not been modified, nor has her personality become integrated, exposing the complex issue of limits in psychoanalytic treatment. The second is a post-autistic girl who has made considerable developmental progress. From being a wild animal-like child, she has blossomed into a passionate, responsive girl despite very severe intellectual and behavioural limitations. She is now capable of much more open and sincere emotional contact. Although there is a wide oscillation in her moods, they can be definitely described as L, H and K (rather than -L, -H and -K of the first patient) pace Bion.
